findings.title: `date | datetime` query params may silently turn a midnight datetime into a whole-day bound
findings.description:
`start` and `end` are declared `date | datetime | None`, and `resolve_window` (`routes/windows.py:38-49`) treats a `date` as a whole-day bound. This is the only place in `src` that uses this union. I could not run code in this session, so I haven't confirmed the behaviour. From my reading of pydantic v2's smart-union rules, I expect a string such as `end=2026-06-01T00:00:00Z` to validate as a `date` in lax mode. Pydantic accepts datetimes with zero time as dates, and on a tie the first union member wins. If that is right, `end` would resolve to `23:59:59.999999` instead of midnight, and a midnight `start` with a non-UTC offset would lose its offset.

No test covers this case. Midnight datetimes in `test_kalshi_timeseries.py:239,265,276` only exercise ordering and reversed ranges, and both outcomes pass those. The load test's `_ceiling_window` uses a midnight `start`, where `date` and `datetime` give the same value. Please add a test with `end=…T00:00:00Z` that asserts the reader receives that exact instant. If it fails, parse the bound explicitly instead of relying on the union.

findings.title: `TradeRecord.from_row` indexes the tuple by position, unlike the candle path
findings.description:
`CandleRecord.from_row` is driven by `CANDLE_COLUMNS`, and the module docstring says a column added there is served here without an edit. `TradeRecord.from_row` instead reads `values[0]` through `values[7]`, which silently depends on the order of `TRADE_COLUMNS` minus `market_ticker` (`trade_repository.py:45-55`). Reordering the columns would swap fields without raising an error, for example `yes_price_dollars` and `no_price_dollars`, which share a type.

The integration test (`test_kalshi_serving.py`, `test_value_count_matches_the_repository_mapping`) checks only the length of the tuple. The unit tests build `TradeRow` by hand in the same positional order, so neither one would catch a reorder. Build the record by zipping `TRADE_VALUE_COLUMNS` with `values`, or add a test that round-trips real DB rows and checks each field by name.

findings.title: `_window` uses a non-empty `extra` dict as a flag to add the `period` predicate
findings.description: `_window` adds `period = %(period)s` only when `extra` is truthy. The same dict supplies the parameter values, so the behaviour depends on a hidden coupling. A future caller passing any other `extra` key would get a `period` predicate with no `period` param, which fails at execution time. A caller passing `{}` for candles would silently drop the period filter. Take an explicit `period: int | None` argument instead, and emit both the clause and the parameter from it.

findings.title: `tape_filtered` re-spells a parameter key it says it doesn't re-spell
findings.description: The docstring says the membership test "is not re-spelled here". The code still hard-codes `selection.params["trades_excluded_categories"]` and the `COALESCE(..., '')` semantics from `selection.py:168-170`. It also relies on the `list` type of the bound value, with a `# pragma: no cover` guard. Renaming that key in `selection.py` would turn this into a `KeyError` at request time. The parametrized integration test would catch it, but this is still a second spelling. Have `selection.py` expose the evaluator or the key as a named constant, as the project's "define it once" rule asks.

findings.title: `_CANDLE_OBJECTS` values are never used
findings.description: Only the keys of `_CANDLE_OBJECTS` are read, in `from_row`. The `type[BaseModel]` values are dead, and the comment says they identify "which object holds them". Either make a `frozenset` of names or use the values to construct the nested objects.

findings.title: Test helpers are long, and a few rely on private details
findings.description: `_seed_kalshi_dense` is about 90 lines, well over the ~50-line guide. The sections (series/events/markets, candles, trades, state rows) split naturally into separate functions. `test_188_kalshi_api_nfr.py` is about 360 lines, over the ~300-line guide. `_RecordingCursor.statements` is a class-level mutable list, and `_client` reaches into `pool._pool`. Both are justified in comments but fragile.

findings.title: Table name is passed as a plain string to `sql.SQL`
findings.description: `_count` builds `sql.SQL(table)` from a `str` parameter and relies on a `noqa: S608` comment saying callers only pass literals. This is safe today, since both callers pass constants. `sql.Identifier("kalshi", "candlesticks")` would remove the need for the suppression.

findings.title: `gaps.py` keeps its own copy of `_window_start_utc`
findings.description: The day-boundary helpers moved into `routes/windows.py` for bars and the Kalshi routes, but `gaps.py` still defines an identical `_window_start_utc`. Its `_window_end_utc` is deliberately different (half-open), so only the start helper is a true duplicate. This is a small DRY leftover. The new `windows.py` docstring warns about this kind of drift.

findings.title: Admission guard, connection scoping and error handling
findings.description: The count runs before the fetch, and no `LIMIT` is applied, so a race can only make a response too long, never silently truncated. One pooled checkout covers seek, count and fetch, and the 422 is raised after the executor returns. The 404, 422 and `RuntimeError` paths all go through the app's existing handlers, and the `RuntimeError` is logged by the process-boundary handler. Unit tests cover ordering, ceiling, connection release, window resolution and serialization. The integration and load tiers use only throwaway databases, and the load tier avoids the production URL variable. Moving the schema helpers into `kalshi_support/schema.py` is consistent across every caller I found.
